messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Tran, a 76-year-old South Eastern Asian man with a long history of working in warehouses, has been experiencing intense and distressing symptoms since his time as a civilian during a war zone conflict decades ago. He recently sought help after finding that his daily life had become increasingly difficult to manage due to the persistent intrusion of memories from that traumatic period. Mr. Tran’s triggers are deeply rooted in specific sensory experiences and situational cues. The feeling of being physically restrained, whether by tight clothing or the close quarters of a crowded space, instantly brings back vivid and terrifying memories of his time in the war zone. Similarly, any confrontation with aggression, even in the form of a heated argument at work, can set off an immediate recall of the intense conflicts he witnessed during the war. The smell of certain chemicals or burning materials further compounds this, as it often serves as a potent reminder of the acrid odors from explosions and fires. The memories that are triggered without warning are so detailed and overwhelming that they leave him feeling paralyzed with emotion. Mr. Tran reports that even in the quiet moments at home, something as simple as a rustling sound or the scent of smoke can instantly transport him back to those harrowing days, where he was constantly on edge, fearing for his life. The vividness of these memories is such that he often finds himself reliving the worst moments with startling clarity. When this happens, Mr. Tran feels so overwhelmed by the intensity of the emotions that he must stop whatever he is doing and take a moment to gather himself. The cycle between triggers and memory is relentless. For example, on one particularly stressful day at work, a coworker’s aggressive demeanor set off a chain reaction. The confrontation triggered a vivid recall of a violent encounter from his war experience. This memory was so overwhelming that Mr. Tran left the warehouse abruptly, unable to continue working because he felt as though he was back in the middle of a conflict zone. The tactile sensation of the tight straps on his work vest, meant for safety, only added to his distress, making him feel restrained and helpless. The same pattern repeats at home, where even seemingly innocuous smells can trigger memories that leave him feeling emotionally drained. For instance, cooking aromas sometimes evoke the smell of burning debris from the war zone. This makes it difficult for him to enjoy meals or social gatherings, as he is constantly on alert for potential triggers. Mr. Tran’s work environment exacerbates his symptoms due to its crowded and often confrontational nature. He has noticed that the physical constraints of wearing protective gear at work can trigger memories that leave him unable to function properly. Consequently, this has led to conflicts with supervisors who do not understand why he is frequently absent or unproductive. Mr. Tran’s life has become a constant vigil for these triggers, and each encounter only deepens his fear and discomfort. The overwhelming emotions from the memories often lead to avoidance behaviors, such as staying away from crowded places and avoiding confrontations at all costs. However, this cycle of heightened awareness and subsequent memory recall leaves him feeling increasingly isolated. Ultimately, what brought Mr. Tran to seek help was the realization that he could no longer cope with these intrusive memories and their triggers without professional assistance. He is most afraid of losing his job due to his inability to manage his symptoms effectively but hopes that therapy can provide some relief and teach him coping strategies to reclaim his life. Mr. Tran’s narrative reflects a deeply intertwined cycle where triggers lead to vivid memory recall, which in turn intensifies future trigger responses, creating a self-perpetuating loop of distress.
